newsitem.title: UK: S&P affirms Ireland ratings, outlook stable.
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms Ireland ratings, outlook stable.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Thursday it affirmed its AA foreign currency sovereign credit rating on the Republic of Ireland, as well as its A1 plus short-term foreign currency rating.

"At the same time, Standard & Poor's has affirmed its AAA long-term and A1 plus short-term local currency sovereign credit ratings on the Republic. The outlook on all long-term ratings is stable," the agency said in a statement.

"The ratings are based on the Republic's adherence to prudent fiscal and other macroeconomic policies, which have significantly reduced the public debt burden and created the conditions for relatively fast economic growth and low inflation," S&P said.

Over the medium term, sustained containment of budget deficits and continued economic growth should lead to further cuts of a still-heavy public debt burden and a fall in high unemployment rates, the agency said.

The AAA local currency rating reflects a stronger capacity to pay Irish pound-denominated debt than foreign currency debt because of the country's taxation powers and control of the domestic financial system, S&P said.
S&P said Ireland's ratings are supported by --
-- Its status as a modern industrial economy with political stability. It said Ireland has benefited EU membership, attracting foreign direct investment and official transfers,

-- A track record of prudent macro policies, as average inflation fell to 2.4 percent last year from more than four percent in 1989 and double-digit deficits in the early 1980s were reduced to an average 2.1 percent of GDP since 1989,

-- and solid external finances. Helped by real export growth averaging more than 10 percent annually for the past 10 years, Ireland's current account surplus is estimated at almost seven percent of GDP this year and is one of the highest among similarly rated countries.
S&P said the foreign currency rating, however, is constrained by --
-- a level of economic development that trails the average for EU countries,
-- and a still high, though declining, public debt burden. Ireland's general government debt peaked in 1986 at 118 percent of GDP and has fallen sharply since then.
"It remains high at 80 percent of GDP, leaving the country somewhat vulnerable to shifts in economic conditions," the S&P statement said.
